---
title: "Wild Cats at the Urban Edge"
subtitle: "Pumas and bobcats in San Francisco Bay Area open spaces"
author: "Kiran Balasubramanian"
date: last-modified
---

Two species share the same ground here, and they present opposite problems.
Bobcats are common and easy to record. Pumas are rare, wide-ranging, and their
precise locations are a risk to publish. One landscape, two data situations that
point in different directions. This project keeps them on separate tracks and
lets each tell its own story.

## Not a recovery story

The sister project to this one studied tiger recovery in India. That study had a
national census: five repeated survey rounds that made "population change over
time" the natural question to ask.

The Bay Area has no equivalent for either species. There is one recent statewide
mountain lion abundance estimate and no statewide bobcat estimate at all. A
recovery narrative is not available, because the census that would support it
does not exist.

What the region does have is dense, well-kept open data on land protection, road
mortality, and landscape structure. So the question changes. This project is
about **distribution and coexistence at the urban–wildland edge** — where the
animals are, how they move, and where their movement meets the roads — not about
recovery over time.

## Ten counties, eight million people

The study area is the ten-county San Francisco Bay Area: Alameda, Contra Costa,
Marin, Napa, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Santa Cruz, Solano, and
Sonoma. Roughly eight million people live inside this frame, next to a patchwork
of parks, watershed lands, ranch easements, and open-space preserves.

Pumas and bobcats persist here at the urban edge, not in wilderness. That edge is
the subject. The relevant questions are about movement, permeability, and
coexistence, not about a return to some earlier state.

## Two species, two tracks

The two species are analysed in parallel and never pooled. This is a fixed rule
of the project (Decision 3), and it follows directly from their data. Pooling
sparse, sensitive puma records with abundant, low-risk bobcat records would hide
the very contrast that makes each track work.

| | Puma | Bobcat |
|---|---|---|
| Occurrence records | Sparse | Abundant |
| Location sensitivity | High — precise points held, coarsened on publish | Low |
| Home range | Very large (100s of km²) | Small (10s of km²) |
| Primary story | Isolation and connectivity | Occupancy and distribution |
| Primary method | Least-cost paths and corridors | Occupancy models, KDE, Gi\* |

The puma track holds 1,028 precise, publicly shared occurrence points inside the
study frame. That number is small for an animal that ranges over hundreds of
square kilometres, so the puma work is built around connectivity: where the core
habitat patches are, and how an animal could move between them. The precise
points are never published — every puma map is generalised first. How that is
done is set out in the sensitive-data policy and shown on each puma figure.

The bobcat track is the opposite. Records are abundant, so the work is about
distribution: which open-space units bobcats occupy, and which landscape
characteristics best explain that pattern.

## Five questions

The analysis is organised around five pre-registered questions. Each belongs to
one track, except the last, which cuts across both:

1. **Landscape.** How is protected open space distributed across the ten counties,
   and how connected or fragmented is it from the view of a wide-ranging carnivore?
2. **Bobcat.** Where are bobcats present across open-space units, and which
   landscape characteristics best explain that pattern?
3. **Puma.** Where are the likely movement corridors between core habitat patches,
   and where do those corridors cross major roads and high-traffic barriers?
4. **Both.** Where do the modelled puma corridors cross major roads and
   high-traffic barriers, and where is wildlife–vehicle collision risk therefore
   concentrated? Direct mortality records are pending; the road crossings serve
   as the interim risk proxy.
5. **Cross-cutting.** How much of the apparent spatial pattern reflects true
   distribution, and how much reflects observer and detection effort?

The fifth question is treated as a first-class result, not a footnote. Detection
effort shapes every descriptive layer in the project, and the two species answer
it in opposite ways: the bobcat model corrects for effort, while the puma
corridors do not depend on it. That contrast runs through the sections that
follow.
